title: The Warning We Keep Skipping: Why Scripture Says “Do Not Be Deceived” Again and Again
paragraphs: The Warning We Keep Skipping: Why Scripture Says “Do Not Be Deceived” Again and Again
The Bible repeats this warning because the most dangerous lie is not always the one you know is false—it is the one you have believed so deeply that you no longer think to question it.
There is a frightening possibility most of us would rather not consider.
You can be sincere… and sincerely wrong.
You can feel peaceful about something that is destroying you.
You can call bondage “freedom.”
You can rename compromise “growth.”
You can mistake applause for confirmation, emotion for revelation, popularity for truth, and religious activity for actually knowing Jesus.
You can even hold a Bible in your hands while resisting what the Bible is trying to tell you.
That is why three words keep appearing like warning lights throughout the New Testament:
Do not be deceived.
In Greek, Paul repeatedly writes:
μὴ πλανᾶσθε — mē planasthe.
“Do not be deceived.” “Do not be led astray.”

The expression appears in passages such as 1 Corinthians 6:9, 1 Corinthians 15:33, and Galatians 6:7. The verb belongs to the family of πλανάω — planaō, carrying the idea of wandering, straying, misleading, or being led away from the right path. In 1 Corinthians 6:9 the Greek text explicitly reads μὴ πλανᾶσθε.
That image matters.
Deception is not always someone grabbing you by the shoulders and announcing, “I am about to ruin your life.”
Sometimes deception simply gets you walking.
One step.
Then another.
Just a few degrees away from truth.
Nothing dramatic happens at first.
You still pray.
You still attend church.
You still post verses.
You still know Christian vocabulary.
You still say, “God knows my heart.”
But somewhere along the road, something changed.
The question stopped being, “Lord, is this true?”
It became, “How can I make this feel acceptable?”
The question stopped being, “What does Scripture say?”
It became, “What interpretation will let me keep what I do not want to surrender?”
And that is precisely why biblical warnings against deception are acts of mercy.
God warns us because deception, by definition, rarely announces itself as deception.
A deceived person normally does not wake up thinking, I am deceived.
They wake up thinking they can see clearly.
That is what makes the subject so terrifying.
And so personal.
Because this article is not primarily about “those people.”
It is about me.
It is about you.
It is about the uncomfortable possibility that there may be something we desperately want to believe because the truth would require something from us.
Jesus Himself warned His disciples this way.
When they asked Him about the signs surrounding His coming and the end of the age, His response begins:
Βλέπετε μή τις ὑμᾶς πλανήσῃ.
Blepete mē tis hymas planēsē.
The sense is: “See to it that no one leads you astray.”
That is Matthew 24:4, and the Greek text confirms the force of the warning: Βλέπετε carries the command to watch or take heed, while πλανήσῃ speaks of misleading or leading astray.
Notice what Jesus did not say.
He did not say deception would only threaten foolish people.
He was speaking to His disciples.
People who followed Him.
People who heard His teaching.
People who had seen His works.
Apparently, proximity to religious truth does not make vigilance unnecessary.
It makes vigilance essential.
And suddenly Scripture's repeated warnings begin making sense.
The Bible warns us about deception because human beings have an extraordinary capacity to believe what protects their desires.
We do it in relationships.
“They'll change.”
We do it with secret sin.
“I can stop whenever I want.”
We do it with bitterness.
“I've forgiven them. I just never want anything good to happen to them.”
We do it with pride.
“I'm not arrogant. I simply know I'm right.”
We do it with greed.
“I just want security.”
We do it with compromise.
“Everybody does it.”
We do it spiritually.
“God understands.”
Yes.
God understands perfectly.
And because He understands perfectly, He loves us enough to tell us the truth.
That is the part our generation desperately needs to recover.
Love and warning are not enemies.
Sometimes warning is love.
A physician who sees something dangerous on a scan does not prove compassion by hiding the diagnosis.
A father who sees his child walking toward traffic does not whisper, “I affirm your journey.”
He shouts.
Not because the child is hated.
Because the child is loved.
Scripture's “Do not be deceived” passages are the voice of divine love refusing to watch human beings walk peacefully toward destruction.
Consider Galatians 6:7.
Paul again begins with the warning:
Μὴ πλανᾶσθε — Mē planasthe.
Then comes the reality we spend much of our lives trying to negotiate:
God is not mocked. A person reaps what he sows.
There is something painfully ordinary about sowing.
Seeds are small.
That is why we underestimate them.
A private click.
A secret conversation.
A little dishonesty.
One more drink when you already know where this road goes.
One flirtation you insist is harmless.
One resentment rehearsed before bed.
One compromise nobody else knows about.
One morning without prayer becomes several.
One week without opening Scripture becomes months.
One excuse becomes a lifestyle.
Seeds.
Tiny things.
Then harvest comes.
And harvest always looks disproportionate until you remember how long the seeds were growing underground.
That is why “Do not be deceived” is not God trying to ruin your pleasure.
It is God standing at the edge of the field saying:
Please understand what these seeds become.
The same pattern appears with remarkable severity in 1 Corinthians 6.
Paul asks whether the Corinthians understand that the unrighteous will not inherit God's kingdom, and then says:
μὴ πλανᾶσθε — do not be deceived.
The warning is serious because sin is serious.
But stopping at verse 10 would mutilate Paul's message.
Because then comes verse 11.
And there, suddenly, the thunderstorm breaks open and grace comes pouring through.

Paul reminds these believers that some of them had been characterized by the very sins he had just named—but they had been washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
Do you see it?
The Gospel does not say sin is imaginary.
The Gospel says sin does not have to have the final word.
Christianity does not save us by changing the definition of darkness.
Christ saves us by bringing us into the light.
Paul's message is not:
“Those terrible people over there should be ashamed.”
It is:
That was some of you.
Were.
There may not be a more beautiful past-tense word in the Christian life.
Were.
You were enslaved.
You were guilty.
You were wandering.
You were hiding.
You were living for yourself.
You were trying to satisfy a hunger with things that only made the hunger deeper.
You were carrying shame into rooms where nobody knew your name for it.
You were smiling in photographs while something inside you was collapsing.
You were pretending.
You were running.
You were lost.
But Jesus Christ entered the sentence.
And when Jesus enters the sentence, were becomes possible.
That is Christianity.
Not self-improvement.
Not religious cosmetics.
Not learning how to hide your wounds underneath church clothes.
Death and resurrection.
Guilt and justification.
Defilement and washing.
Slavery and freedom.
Scandal and grace.
Maybe that is why this subject hurts.
Because somewhere beneath our theological discussions, many of us already know where we have been deceiving ourselves.
You know the conversation you need to end.
You know the habit you keep deleting from your history but not from your life.
You know the resentment you have baptized as “discernment.”
You know whether your public Christianity resembles your private Christianity.
You know the thing you hope nobody ever asks about.
You know the prayer you are afraid to pray because you suspect obedience may cost you something.
Maybe your greatest deception is not that you stopped believing in God.
Maybe it is that you learned how to keep believing in God without allowing Him to contradict you.
Read that again.
Because deception does not always make an atheist.
Sometimes it makes a religious person who has placed himself on God's throne.
That is why Scripture must remain above us rather than beneath us.
If I only accept biblical truth when it agrees with me, Scripture is not my authority.
I am.
If Jesus is Lord only when His commands match my preferences, my preferences are actually lord.
The Gospel confronts that illusion.
Jesus did not come merely to decorate our existing identities with Christian vocabulary.
He calls us to Himself.
“Follow Me.”
Those words contain both death and life.
Death to self-rule.
Life in Christ.
Death to the illusion that I belong to myself.
Life under the King who loved me enough to give Himself for me.
This is why biblical repentance is so beautiful when properly understood.
Repentance is not purchasing forgiveness by becoming miserable enough.
Repentance is turning.
Coming home.
Dropping the weapon.
Opening the locked room.
Agreeing with God about the darkness because you have finally seen the Light standing in front of you.
And the Light has a name.
Jesus.
The Christian answer to deception is therefore not paranoia.
It is not spending your life obsessed with identifying everybody else's errors.
There is a strange irony in becoming an expert on everyone else's deception while remaining blind to your own pride.
The answer is Christ-centered vigilance.
Scripture.
Prayer.
Humility.
A teachable heart.
The fellowship of believers.
Testing what we hear rather than swallowing every spiritual-sounding claim.
And above everything else, abiding in Jesus Christ.
Because deception thrives wherever truth becomes negotiable.
This matters especially now.
We live in an age where algorithms learn what keeps our attention and repeatedly place similar material before us. Eventually, familiarity can begin to feel like confirmation.
But repetition does not make something true.
Virality does not make something true.
A million likes cannot turn falsehood into truth.
A preacher's confidence cannot make an interpretation biblical.
A Christian label cannot sanctify an idea.
Your feelings cannot rewrite God's character.
And this article should not receive a free pass either.
Check what you read here against Scripture.
Open the Bible.
Read the surrounding chapters.
Look at context.
Ask what the author actually intended to communicate.
Let Scripture correct the writer, the preacher, the influencer, the tradition, the culture—and you.
And me.
Especially me.
Because one of the safest prayers a Christian can pray may also be one of the most frightening:
“Jesus, show me where I am wrong.”
Not where they are wrong.
Where I am wrong.
Show me what I have excused.
Show me what I have renamed.
Show me where pride has disguised itself as conviction.
Show me where fear has disguised itself as wisdom.
Show me where bitterness has disguised itself as justice.
Show me where lust has disguised itself as love.
Show me where greed has disguised itself as ambition.
Show me where cowardice has disguised itself as peace.
Show me where religion has become a substitute for knowing You.
And then, Lord…
lead me home.
Perhaps you are reading this with something already rising inside you.
A memory.
A name.
A habit.
A compromise.
Something hidden.
Do not run from conviction.
But do not confuse conviction with hopeless condemnation either.
Look again at 1 Corinthians 6.
The warning is real.
The sin is real.
The consequences are real.
And then:
“Such were some of you.”
Grace does not deny the scandal.
Grace rewrites what happens after it.
Peter denied Jesus.
The thief beside Christ reached the final hours of a ruined life.
Paul had persecuted the church.
The Corinthians carried histories Paul could describe without pretending those histories were harmless.
Yet the center of Christianity has never been the impressive moral résumé of redeemed people.
The center is the crucified and risen Christ.
At Calvary, God did not shrug at sin.
Jesus bore judgment.
At the empty tomb, death did not receive the last word.
Christ rose.
And now forgiveness is not offered because sin does not matter.
Forgiveness is offered because Jesus Christ has done what sinners could never do for themselves.
That means you do not need to hide in order to come to Him.
You need to come honestly.
No performance.
No carefully edited testimony.
No spiritual résumé.
No pretending.
Repent and believe the Gospel.
Bring the real thing into the light.
The addiction.
The pride.
The sexual sin.
The secret messages.
The envy.
The unbelief.
The rage.
The greed.
The religious hypocrisy.
The years you wasted.
The thing you swore you would never do again and then did again.
Bring that person to Jesus.
Because that is the person who needs grace.
And grace is not permission to remain chained.
Grace is the undeserved mercy of God that receives sinners and begins transforming them.
This is where “Do not be deceived” becomes unexpectedly beautiful.
God exposes the lie because He wants you free.
He tells you the road is wrong because there is still time to turn around.
He names the poison because He is offering life.
He turns the lights on because He is not afraid of what they reveal.
Jesus already knew the worst thing about you when He went to the cross.
You are not going to shock Him with your confession.
But you cannot experience the freedom of bringing something into His light while continually insisting that darkness is light.
So perhaps the question is no longer, “Why does Scripture say ‘Do not be deceived’ so often?”
Perhaps the question is:
What does God love us enough to keep warning us about?
The answer is devastating and beautiful.
He knows how easily we wander.
And He still calls wanderers home.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to explain the details publicly.
There is no shame in admitting you need prayer.
Someone reading silently may desperately need to discover that “such were some of you” can become their story too.
Send it privately to the believer who has been drifting.
Send it to the person asking hard questions.
Send it to the Christian who feels too ashamed to come home.
We glorify God through faith in Christ and lives of worship, obedience, love, generosity, and faithful stewardship.
Not because an algorithm is our savior.
Jesus is.
But because behind screens are real human beings.
Real marriages breaking.
Real teenagers confused.
Real Christians secretly drowning.
Real skeptics searching.
Real prodigals wondering whether God would still receive them.
Let that possibility make sharing feel less like promotion and more like mission.
We cannot force anybody to believe.
We cannot manipulate anybody into repentance.
We cannot save a soul.
But we can refuse to hide the light we have been given.
We can tell the truth.
We can point toward Christ.
We can say, “I was wandering too.”
We can say, “Jesus found me.”
We can say, “There is still mercy.”
We can say, “Come home.”
And when Scripture says “Do not be deceived,” perhaps we should finally hear the heart behind the warning.
Not the voice of a God searching for an excuse to reject sinners.
The voice of the Shepherd calling wandering sheep away from the cliff.
Truth is not always comfortable.
But neither is a surgeon's knife.
Some wounds heal because somebody loved us enough to cut away what was killing us.
So when God's Word exposes you, do not immediately silence the discomfort.
Ask what the discomfort is revealing.
Open Scripture.
Look at Jesus.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Receive the grace you cannot earn.
Then get up and follow Him.
Because the most frightening deception may be believing you are safe while wandering away from Christ.
And one of the sweetest moments of grace is discovering that when the truth finally exposes where you have wandered…
the Shepherd is already calling your name.
